title: Cap. X Arg. X reply: question is predestinating will to do or not do — God gave Peter faith eternally willed; not giving Judas proves preterition/reprobation
pass_a_gloss: I answer that Corvinus is plainly forgetful of the matter under dispute. For the question is not of God’s will under any notion whatever, but of the will of God predestinating to do something or not to do it. And it is the best and firmest consequence; God gave faith, perseverance, and everlasting life unto Peter, Therefore by a predestinating will from eternity he willed to give him faith, perseverance and everlasting life. And on the contrary that is no less firm: God did not give unto Judas faith, perseverance and everlasting life: Therefore he passed him by, did not predestinate him, reprobated him, was unwilling to affect him with such great goods.
pass_b_english: I answer: Corvinus has plainly forgotten what is under dispute. The question is not God’s will under any notion, but God’s will as predestinating to do or not do. This consequence is best and firmest: God gave Peter faith, perseverance, and everlasting life; therefore by predestinating will from eternity he willed to give him those goods. No less firm the reverse: God did not give Judas faith, perseverance, and everlasting life; therefore he passed him by, did not predestine him, reprobated him, and would not affect him with such great goods.
source_text: Respondeo, Corvinum immemorem plane esse qua de re disputetur. Non enim quaestio est de voluntate Dei sub qualibet notione, sed de voluntate Dei praedestinantis aliquid facere aut non facere. Est autem optima et firmissima consequentia; Deus dedit fidem, perseverantiam, et vitam aeternam Petro, Ergo voluntate praedestinante ab aeterno voluit illi dare fidem, perseverantiam et vitam aeternam. Et e contra non minus firma est illa: Deus non dedit Judae fidem, perseverantiam et vitam aeternam: Ergo illum praeteriit, non praedestinavit, reprobavit, tantis bonis afficere noluit.
